title: Human nuclear ribomes reveal DNA-embedded ribonucleotides as epigenetic modulators of transcription-associated DNA supercoiling.

verified.what_i_actually_checked: Found GEO series GSE297046 (40 samples) and GSE333819 (9 samples) by title search, since PubMed elink returned none. Read both GEO file lists: per-sample strand-split bedgraphs (0.8–124 MB each, gzipped), 4 bisulfite bigwigs (~370 MB each), RAW tars of 2.4 GB and 183 MB. Downloaded and parsed GSE297046_DNA_rez_500K_counts.tsv.gz (46,080 rows: 4 fragmentation types x 500 kb bins x strand, raw counts), GSE297046_HEK_tpm.csv.gz (18,656 genes x 6 HEK293T samples, TPM), GSE333819 TPM table (20,048 genes x 10 samples incl. TOP1 siRNA). Opened one ribose-seq bedgraph (FS326, HEK293T WT dsF rep1, + strand): 127,465 lines, 127,663 rNMP counts, single-nucleotide intervals on chr names hg38-style. Parsed GEO sample metadata: CD4+ T cells, hESC-H9 and HEK293T WT plus 2 RNASEH2A knockout clones, with 4 fragmentation schemes (dsF, RE1, RE2, RE3).
verified.what_came_from_paper_text_only: No full text available (Cell, no PMCID; Europe PMC full-text call returned HTTP 500). The ~1 million rNMPs per genome, ribonucleotide-enriched zones near TSSs, CpG/R-loop/G4 overlap and supercoiling findings come from the abstract only. Genome build is assumed hg38 from chromosome naming, not confirmed. Which fragmentation enzymes RE1–RE3 are, and how background DNA-seq normalisation was done, were not verified.

a1_downloadable.note: Public GEO, no login; small processed tables and per-sample bedgraphs download directly (checked).

a2_label_is_a_column.note: Partly: the per-nucleotide rNMP count is a column in each bedgraph, but a usable label (rNMP density per window or per TSS) must be built by binning one track and ideally normalising to matched background DNA-seq. That is aggregating one measurement, not a cross-source join.

a3_inputs_present.note: Inputs are DNA sequence from the hg38 reference genome by coordinate; one reference download, no per-item lookups. Gene TPM tables carry Ensembl IDs (checked).

a4_units_stated.note: Bedgraph value is a count of captured rNMP ends per position (checked: integers, sum matches line count). TPM (transcripts per million) tables are labelled. Normalisation to library size is our decision.

a5_enough_rows.note: One sparse WT sample already has 127,465 rNMP positions; genome-wide 1 kb bins (~3 million) or ~20,000 promoter windows give far more than 1,500 labelled rows. Counts per window are low in WT, so noise is the real constraint.

a6_fits_laptop.working_set: ~1 GB of bedgraphs for ~20 ribose-seq samples, reduced to a <100 MB window table
a6_fits_laptop.note: Skip the 2.4 GB RAW tar and bisulfite bigwigs; stream individual bedgraphs. Largest single file 124 MB, above the 50 MB cap, so fetch it deliberately or pick smaller replicates.

a7_counts_match_paper.note: Cannot fully check: no full text. GEO sample counts (40 + 9) are internally consistent; the one WT sample I opened holds ~0.13 million rNMPs, below the abstract's ~1 million per genome, plausibly because that is one strand of one shallow library.

a8_label_provenance.note: Label is a physical measurement (ribose-seq capture of rNMP 3' ends, sequenced). Caveat: restriction-enzyme fragmentation imposes cut-site bias that a sequence model can learn, so use dsF samples or RE-matched background as a control.

B1.why: Per-sample strand-split bedgraphs plus metadata; join on coordinates after binning. Checked file lists.

B2.why: Bedgraph and TSV/CSV tables parsed first try with standard tools (checked).

B3.why: Libraries differ in depth (0.8–124 MB files) and fragmentation enzyme; need depth and background normalisation.

B4.why: Integer counts, no censored or qualitative values (checked one bedgraph).

B5.why: One record per position per strand per sample; no duplicates seen in the opened file.

B6.why: GEO metadata names cell, genotype, fragmentation; RE1–RE3 enzymes and processing not documented in what I read.

C1.why: Cross-cell-type transfer of sequence-predicted rNMP density is informative either way: sequence-intrinsic versus cell-state-driven.

C2.why: Searches found no sequence-to-rNMP-density model; only mapping tools (Ribose-Map) and nanopore detection.

C3.why: Likely novel: first human genome-wide rNMP maps across three cell types and RNase H2 knockouts.

C4.why: Ribose-seq is a specialised multi-day wet-lab protocol practised by few labs.

C5.why: No published predictive number; obvious baselines are GC/CpG content and dinucleotide context models.

D1.why: Nucleotide Transformer and DNABERT-2 are open-weight DNA language models; AlphaGenome also available.

D2.why: Embed ~20,000–100,000 short windows once on CPU, then fit a regression head.

D3.why: Nucleotide Transformer CC BY-NC-SA, AlphaGenome non-commercial; DNABERT-2 Apache-2.0.

E1.why: Hold out chromosomes, and hold out a whole cell type (CD4T vs hESC vs HEK293T).

E2.why: 22 autosomes and 3 cell types plus 2 knockout clones give enough holdout groups.

E3.why: Per-window GC content or genome-wide mean density is a trivial dummy.

E4.why: Replicates exist (e.g. HEK293T dsF reps 1–2, CD4T dsF+RE1 reps 1–3), so replicate correlation sets ceiling.

E5.why: Known effects: enrichment at CpG islands/TSSs and higher rGMP in RNASEH2A knockout (abstract).

E6.why: Label shuffle, and a restriction-site-only feature model to expose fragmentation artifacts.

E7.why: Held-out cell type within data; possibly other labs' human emRiboSeq/HydEn-seq maps (not verified).

E8.why: Paper reports enrichment statistics, not a predictive score to reproduce; full text unread.

G1.why: Genomic coordinates (hg38-style names, build unconfirmed) and Ensembl gene IDs in TPM tables (checked).

G2.why: ENCODE tracks for H9/HEK293 (CpG, H3K4me3, DNase), G4 and R-loop maps, joinable on coordinates.

G3.why: Window-to-track overlap is clean on fixed bins once genome build is fixed.

G4.why: Does sequence alone or chromatin/transcription explain rNMP density? Partly done descriptively in paper.

H1.why: Genome-wide maps record zero-count regions too, so low-density windows are true negatives.

H2.why: One lab, three cell types, one capture protocol.

H4.why: Fragmentation-enzyme bias is implied by multiple RE schemes; full discussion unread.

I1.why: Storici lab (Georgia Tech) and the RNase H2 / Aicardi-Goutières syndrome community.

I2.why: Could prioritise loci for follow-up, or substitute for mapping in cell types not assayed.

I3.why: Correlation of predicted versus measured density roughly matches 'where are rNMPs enriched'.

I4.why: GC/CpG content may explain most variance; must test the simple rule first.

J1.why: DNA language-model embeddings, chromosome and cell-type holdouts, transfer evaluation.

J2.why: Genomics-literate reasoning possible; rNMP biology is niche.

J3.why: A clean binned ribome table plus a GC-baseline result is shareable at stage one.

backbone.name: Nucleotide Transformer v2 (50M–100M) or DNABERT-2, DNA language models; AlphaGenome as optional comparison
backbone.hardware: Laptop CPU for small checkpoints on ~1–2 kb windows
backbone.licence: Nucleotide Transformer CC BY-NC-SA 4.0; DNABERT-2 Apache-2.0; AlphaGenome non-commercial

integration.partner_dataset: ENCODE chromatin tracks (H3K4me3, DNase) and RNA-seq for H9 and HEK293, plus the paper's own TPM tables
integration.join_key: Genomic coordinates (hg38) and Ensembl gene ID
integration.bigger_question_one_sentence: How much of where ribonucleotides sit in human DNA is written in the sequence itself versus set by cell-specific transcription and chromatin?

controls.positive_control: Model must recover enrichment at CpG islands and TSSs and the higher rNMP load in RNASEH2A knockout; trivially learnable target: GC content of the window.
controls.negative_control: Label shuffle; model using only distance to restriction-enzyme cut sites, to show how much is fragmentation artifact.
controls.external_validation: Train on two cell types, test on the third (held-out cell type); held-out chromosomes.

honest_claim_h3: Predicts relative ribose-seq rNMP capture density per genomic window in three human cell types from one lab, including any residual fragmentation-enzyme bias, not absolute rNMP incorporation in vivo.

plain_idea.one_liner: Use the DNA sequence of a genomic window to predict how many ribonucleotides are embedded there, and test whether this transfers between cell types.
plain_idea.train_on: DNA sequence windows (e.g. 1 kb) from the human reference genome, each with an rNMP count from ribose-seq; genome-wide that is millions of windows, or ~20,000 promoter windows.
plain_idea.predict: The normalised number of embedded ribonucleotides in that window, measured by ribose-seq (a method that captures and sequences the DNA ends at each embedded ribonucleotide).
plain_idea.why_worthwhile: Tells DNA-repair and RNase H2 researchers whether ribonucleotide placement is mostly sequence-encoded (so predictable in unmapped cells) or cell-state-driven; either answer is informative.

label_elsewhere.sources: Earlier ribose-seq maps from the same lab (yeast, e.g. GEO GSE240399, seen in search) and human emRiboSeq/HydEn-seq studies from other labs (known methods, human datasets not verified).
label_elsewhere.why: Another lab's human rNMP map would allow a true cross-protocol external test, but such sets are few and hard to align.

ambitious.why: Publishes rNMP/ribose-seq biology and computational genomics; needs a model that transfers across cell types and separates sequence from chromatin effects.

realistic.why: Fits a first predictive model of human rNMP density with honest cross-cell-type evaluation and artifact controls.

fallback.journal: bioRxiv preprint plus a machine learning in computational biology workshop
fallback.why: Even 'GC content explains it all' or 'fragmentation bias dominates' is a useful negative note.

pitch.headline: First human genome-wide ribonucleotide maps, single-nucleotide and strand-resolved, across 3 cell types plus RNase H2 knockouts, public on GEO with no predictive model yet.
pitch.what_makes_the_data_unusual: ~30 ribose-seq libraries (checked file list) over CD4 T cells, H9 stem cells and HEK293T, 2 knockout clones, 4 fragmentation schemes, plus matched RNA-seq; only one lab produces such data.
pitch.the_win: A frozen DNA-language-model head beating a GC/CpG baseline on held-out chromosomes and transferring to an unseen cell type, approaching the replicate-to-replicate correlation ceiling.
pitch.even_if_it_fails: We learn whether rNMP placement is just GC content or restriction-enzyme bias, which bounds what the paper's 'epigenetic mark' claim can mean.
pitch.who_wants_it: Storici lab (Georgia Tech) and RNase H2 / Aicardi-Goutières syndrome researchers deciding whether to map new cell types or predict them.

ml_idea: Bin ribose-seq bedgraphs into strand-specific windows, normalise to depth and fragmentation background, embed window sequence with a frozen DNA language model, fit a regression head; evaluate on held-out chromosomes and held-out cell types against GC/CpG and k-mer baselines, with a restriction-site-only artifact control.

effort.compute_note: Estimated, not timed: ~50,000 1 kb windows at ~5 windows/s on CPU for a 50M-parameter model; bedgraph sizes taken from GEO file list.
effort.cheapest_killing_check: Bin two replicate WT dsF bedgraphs (e.g. HEK293T reps 1 and 2) into 1 kb windows and compute replicate correlation and how much a GC-content-only model explains; if replicates barely agree or GC explains nearly all, stop.

verdict_reason: Public, parseable, likely-novel rNMP maps with a clean DNA-sequence backbone fit, but wild-type libraries are sparse (~0.13 million rNMPs in the one opened) and restriction-enzyme bias may dominate; check replicate agreement and a GC-only baseline first.
